subject: VAL
label: Grade 11 Humanities
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 11 Humanities Values and life skills, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 2 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Values, ethics and wellbeing
modules.outcome: apply an ethical framework to a case
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Values, ethics and wellbeing', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: apply an ethical framework to a case. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Values, ethics and wellbeing' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: apply an ethical framework to a case. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Calm routine: name the feeling, breathe in for 4 counts and out for 6, talk to someone, do one small helpful thing. Plan screen time: 1 hour, then a 10-minute break. Method: Model run for 'Values, ethics and wellbeing'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Apply an ethical framework to a case: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Learn three lenses. Consequences asks which choice produces the most good for the people affected. Duties asks which rules, rights or promises must be respected. Character asks what a fair, honest, caring person would do. Use all three before you decide.

Step 2, Read a humanities case. A town council has 120,000 to spend. A footbridge repair serves 900 people a week, including children walking to school. A youth centre serves 150 people a week. Spending all 120,000 on the bridge costs 120,000 divided by 900, about 133 per weekly user; on the centre it is 120,000 divided by 150, which is 800.

Step 3, Apply consequences. The bridge helps 900 weekly users, which is 6 times as many as the 150 the youth centre helps. A damaged bridge may also cause accidents. The centre would help a smaller group, though possibly with deeper benefit. Compare size and depth of benefit.

Step 4, Apply duties and character. A council has a duty to keep public routes safe and to treat all groups fairly, including young people. A fair leader would listen to both groups, explain the choice openly and look for other funds for the centre.

Step 5, Decide and justify. Write: 'The council should repair the bridge first, because safety and benefit to the greatest number matter, and then seek funds for the centre.' Note the weakness: it leaves a smaller group waiting, so give a clear timeline.

Step 6, Your turn: a library can open late either for 300 students a week or for 60 adults on a night shift. Which lens gives which answer? Answer: consequences favours 300 students, duty to serve all fairly suggests a mix, character suggests listening to both groups.

points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Career and higher-study pathways' and say what it means in your own words.

modules.example: Solved: List 3 strengths, 3 interests and 3 job families; match one to a course and write a next step with a date. Method: Model run for 'Career and higher-study pathways'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Map interests to courses and careers: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Self-assessment: Dalia rates her interests from 1 to 5: History 5 (reads historical novels), Writing 4 (school magazine), Debate 3, Numbers 2. She backs each rating with an activity she has actually done.
Step 2, Course profiles: Weights for history, writing, debate and numbers. History and archaeology 0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1. Journalism 0.2, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1. Law 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.1. Each row sums to 1.
Step 3, Score History and archaeology: 5 times 0.5 is 2.5; 4 times 0.3 is 1.2; 3 times 0.1 is 0.3; 2 times 0.1 is 0.2. Total is 2.5 plus 1.2 plus 0.3 plus 0.2, so 4.2 out of 5.

Step 4, Score the others: Journalism is 1.0 plus 2.0 plus 0.6 plus 0.2, which is 3.8. Law is 1.0 plus 1.2 plus 1.2 plus 0.2, which is 3.6. The three courses rank 4.2, 3.8 and 3.6, so all three deserve a look.

Step 5, Check the details: Dalia reads the subject needs for each course, notes that law needs strong reading and argument marks and journalism needs a writing portfolio, and talks to a museum curator and a school magazine editor.

Step 6, Plan: She lists a first choice, history, and a second choice, journalism, and plans to publish 3 articles this term as a portfolio. Scores are only a guide, and she will update them as her interests and results change.

Your turn: Ratings History 3, Writing 5, Debate 4, Numbers 2 with Journalism weights 0.2, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1. Model answer: 0.6 plus 2.5 plus 0.8 plus 0.2 is 4.1 out of 5, so journalism is a strong option to explore.

ladder: L1: kindness, honesty and sharing in daily life.
L2: responsibility, courage and care for others and nature.
L3: fairness, respect for difference and service.
L5: leadership, wellbeing and ethical reasoning.
L6 (degree): applied ethics, culture and community work.
L7 (postgraduate): scholarship, counselling or teaching at depth.
